I may represent the majority, minority, or just myself here; I don't have a clue.

When I use a website, I use it because it is useful to me in one way or another. That could mean (not limited to):

  • It provides me with a service I need or want.
  • It gives me a sense of community or family.
  • It entertains me.

I'm bringing this topic up due to a recent controversy, when GitHub recently adopted the Open Code of Conduct[1] for its own repositories and not globally (which seems to be the biggest misunderstanding).

I hold the view that, since this code of conduct is not applied to any repositories I participate in, therefore not having a measureable impact on my daily use of GitHub, I should not seize my use of the service, since it is still useful to me. I feel that moving to an alternative due to an issue like this is melodramatic and isn't the best reaction to a situation like this.

In the same vein, I have a similar view with Reddit: Since this apparent censorship does not affect me, I don't feel the need to leave the site and still find a few subreddits useful. View altered.[2] I still find some subreddits useful enough not to leave, though.

In summary: I want to know why it is a good idea to boycott a website, service, or product that is still useful but only differs in an aspect that has no impact on me as an individual.
On the idea for one to leave a company or website, due to a difference in view that, largely, does not affect one.

First they came for the Socialists, and I did not speak out— Because I was not a Socialist.

Then they came for the Trade Unionists, and I did not speak out— Because I was not a Trade Unionist.

Then they came for the Jews, and I did not speak out— Because I was not a Jew.

Then they came for me—and there was no one left to speak for me.

I don't believe this is applicable in this situation, since alternatives exist and competition is the name of the game on the Internet. If, for example, GitHub were to make all repositories adopt the Open Code of Conduct, then it would be reasonable to move to an alternative because we have that choice.

Since the Internet is free and there will always be the demand for a better service, alternatives will always exist. Services like GitHub, therefore, cannot adopt restrictive policies and still expect the massive userbase they have now.

Very valid. The point I was trying to make is that, if something affects someone else in a negative way but doesn't affect you, you should still stand up for them. On reddit, I had no love for FatPeopleHate yet I supported them when they got shut down along with all the other subs. I may not agree with their viewpoints but they deserve the same rights as anyone else.

As demonstrated by the popular copypasta that Arotaes_Forgehammer posted so quickly, most people who leave in protest are afraid of the same measures being used against them in the future.

For your GitHub example, they recently forced one group to rename their assembly from "WebM for Retards" because a few people complained about it being offensive.[1][2] If they're threatening to remove repos for reasons that retarded, they may remove any repo that a few randoms decide to dislike. (Because of this fear, I'll be moving all my projects to Bitbucket soon, including Veuwer.)

In reddit's case, their changes have already affected us, because they're controlling conversation, which directly affects the information we hear and the opinions we hold. So I think your premise there is flawed.

Also, while it's not always fair, using a website can be seen as implicit support for the values that website represents. This can hurt a person's reputation, but more importantly, the numbers can be used as justification for more extreme actions. Leaving, however, is a very clear statement of opposition, which can be used to condemn and even revert those actions.

Basically, "every man for himself" doesn't work very well. It's better to show some solidarity when other people are taking shit and shouldn't be.

I would argue that it does in fact affect you. When the conversation is controlled, the environment becomes more of an echo chamber. You are no longer exposed to a wealth of ideas and opinions, and only instead see the opinions that Reddit wants you to see. Now if that doesn't bother you, okay, that's fine. Perhaps you have a high threshold for the amount of voices that need to be censored before you consider it to be a problem. But you can't really say it doesn't affect you.

In a similar vein, a single neighbor being robbed doesn't affect you. You can make that claim, sure, and keep ignoring the problem by not contributing to the neighborhood watch fees. Until you wake up one day and realize you live in a crime-infested area and your home value is nothing.

Your first example, with Reddit, has altered my view. I no longer hold the opinion that the censorship does not affects me.

However, I have an issue with your second example. Perhaps I should clarify in my post, but I only hold this view in the scope of a highly competitive and alternative-rich environment, which some parts of the Internet can be, including GitHub.

As I've stated in another comment thread:

I don't believe this is applicable in this situation, since alternatives exist and competition is the name of the game on the Internet. If, for example, GitHub were to make all repositories adopt the Open Code of Conduct, then it would be reasonable to move to an alternative because we have that choice.

Since the Internet is free and there will always be the demand for a better service, alternatives will always exist. Services like GitHub, therefore, cannot adopt restrictive policies and still expect the massive userbase they have now

[Source]

I don't believe that the famous "slowly taking away x until x no longer exists" example is viable or relevant here, since there are many alternatives to the web services or products I use every day. The services enacting a restrictive policy would give me a good reason to find an alternative.

I see what you mean now. To be honest, in reference to the GitHub discussion, I don't know enough about it to be able to give an opinion. I can say though that Reddit publicly and consistently boasted itself to be a bastion of free speech, only to reel in that line in the recent months. GitHub, I'm not sure if it ever made such a boast.

I don't disagree with you for the most part, but in the case of Reddit:

Since this apparent censorship does not affect me, I don't feel the need to leave the site and still find a few subreddits useful.

As a news aggregator site, cutting out free speech and driving conversation as a result of policy in a for profit corporation is absolutely against my best interests. It may be subtle, or it may not be nefarious at all. I don't think worse of you for staying, honestly, and feel a bit reactionary myself for leaving it behind, but the principle matters to me. I don't watch Tom Cruise movies for the same reason. It may be infinitesimal, but I am casting my vote with my presence and my pocketbook.
Well I guess it would come down to values, principles, and convictions. If you strongly disagree with an issue that doesn't affect you personally should you speak out and try to change it?
